title: A Cue’s Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers

paper.title:
A Cue’s Hidden Price:
Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user’s behalf, which lets
seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend.
That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller
content shifts an agent’s choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the
choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice
rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a
counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product’s price until it is
chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue’s price-equivalent: a formally
defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this
way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits
substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 113{,}472 trials, seven
models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev , which outputs a choice probability directly instead of
generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues
yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark
that reports each model’s cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and
auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Large language models are moving from answering questions to acting , as shopping agents that browse, compare, and buy on a user’s behalf. When a model rather than a person makes the choice, a seller’s leverage shifts from persuading a human to steering an agent. Seller-controlled cues such as a “best-seller” claim, an endorsement, or a framed specification can tilt an agent’s recommendation. Such a cue acts like a hidden discount: it makes the agent more likely to choose the product, just as a lower price would, yet no price changes and the buyer never sees it (Figure 1 ). As agentic commerce scales, how much such content shifts an agent’s choice becomes an economically consequential quantity. It matters whether one audits and governs these agents or optimizes content for them, and comparing it across cues requires a common scale . Prior work establishes that LLM shopping agents are susceptible to such cues and that presentation can move them ( Cherep et al., 2026a ; Filandrianos et al., 2025 ; Cherep et al., 2026b ) . It mostly reports their effects as shifts in choice probability, however, and this scale can mislead exactly where it matters. Strong cues saturate the choice near 100 % 100\% and become indistinguishable, and a counterbalanced first-option bias averages to a 50 % 50\% rate that looks like indifference. What such rates leave out is the price that offsets a cue’s influence. Knowing that a cue “raises selection” says nothing about whether it is worth a few cents or a large fraction of the product’s price. We therefore treat a cue’s effect as a hidden price and measure it directly, rather than inferring it from matched response rates ( Chu and Hou, 2026 ) . In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product’s price until it is chosen only half the time. We call that premium the cue’s price-equivalent (PE): the price premium that just offsets the cue’s pull on the agent’s recommendation. Price-equivalent auditing turns qualitative susceptibility into a single monetary number and places text and framing cues on one comparable scale. Figure 1. Auditing a cue as a hidden price (schematic). Three-panel schematic of price-equivalent auditing: an agent prefers a cued product at equal price; a price sweep locates each sentence's price-equivalent; a cue and a neutral sentence are both chosen near 100\% of the time yet differ sixfold in price-equivalent. We price single-sentence cues that a seller can place in a listing. They include endorsements that carry information (authority, social proof, e.g. “chosen by over 10,000 customers”), scarcity claims (“only a few left in stock”), and number-preserving reframings of the same facts (gain/loss, rating rescaling, percent/fraction), and they draw on classic accounts of influence ( Cialdini, 1984 ) and framing ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1981 ) . We also price option order, a channel the platform rather than the seller controls. We use persuasion as a motivating umbrella. PE audits seller-controlled influence relative to price and does not by itself show that a cue induces an irrational bias. For information-bearing cues, PE captures the combined effect of information and presentation. For information-preserving framing, it isolates presentation. Both matter for auditing what a seller can change, even though they are interpreted differently.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (1) The price-equivalent, formally defined and audited. We define a cue’s price-equivalent as a money-denominated selection-parity threshold: the price premium at which the cued product’s selection share, averaged over a balanced presentation policy, falls to one half. We give a nonparametric definition with conditions for existence and censoring, and a single-index model in which the cue enters as an additive utility term. Around it we build a reusable, counterbalanced audit protocol with a cue-free price-sensitivity control and a primacy diagnostic. The protocol applies unchanged across cues, models, and categories, and it even prices a non-linguistic intervention that the platform controls: option order (Section 3 ). (2) What priced auditing reveals. Across 113,472 113{,}472 trials, seven models, and two categories, a price axis resolves what an equal-price choice rate cannot. Six cue conditions are each chosen in at least 95 % 95\% of trials and are thus indistinguishable at equal price, yet their price-equivalents range from 1.6 % 1.6\% to 21.4 % 21.4\% . The equal-price ranking can even invert: gain/loss framing commands one of the largest premiums but is chosen less often than scarcity. The resulting susceptibility profile is selective and model-specific, and it replicates in a second category. The same pricing turns the well-documented first-option (primacy) bias from a nuisance into a priced channel that the platform controls. Because this bias can look like indifference, it is a caution for any choice-based evaluation of agents, including LLM-as-judge (Section 4 ). (3) The first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model. We apply the instrument to Jev , a model that returns a choice probability directly instead of generating text. The equal-price ceiling and its resolution by price reappear, so they are not artifacts of text generation. Jev also shows a susceptibility profile of its own: it resists most cues but is moved by the strongest social-proof claims (Section 4.7 ). As a resource, we release the stimuli, prompts, seeds, per-trial logs, and code as a benchmark that others can run on new models and categories. 1 1 1 https://github.com/Flexxbo/price-equivalent-auditing It reports each model’s cue-price profile rather than a single score, because raw PE must be read alongside price sensitivity and therefore resists a single cross-model ranking (Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: LLM agents in shopping and consumer choice.
sections.text: WebShop and VisualWebArena established web shopping as an agent-evaluation setting, but measure task completion and grounding rather than how seller-controlled content changes preferences ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Koh et al., 2024 ) . On a benchmark built from 31,865 31{,}865 real online-shopping sessions, prompt-only LLMs poorly predict users’ next actions, with the strongest baseline reaching 11.86 % 11.86\% accuracy, and tend to generate more purchases than the observed users ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . Recent conceptual work argues that classical consumer frameworks must evolve as LLM agents increasingly act on users’ behalf, which leaves the steerability of agent choices an open question ( Reusens et al., 2026a ) . That such choices can be steered is well documented. Closest to our setting, ABxLab manipulates prices, ratings, product order, and textual nudges across multiple LLM agents and finds large and predictable shifts in choice ( Cherep et al., 2026a ) . Bias Beware frames cognitive-bias cues as black-box attacks on recommender systems ( Filandrianos et al., 2025 ) , Visual Persuasion shows that image edits steer vision-language model choices ( Cherep et al., 2026b ) , and altering only an item’s title can raise its exposure in LLM-based recommenders while leaving overall recommendation performance largely unchanged ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . The incentive is not hypothetical. Crafted page content can make production search assistants promote one seller’s products and discredit competitors’, creating a prisoner’s-dilemma-like dynamic in which recommendation rates fall for all products as attacks proliferate ( Nestaas et al., 2024 ) . Optimising content for generative engines has already been formalised as Generative Engine Optimization ( Aggarwal et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Persuasion and behavioural bias in LLMs.
sections.text: The cues we study draw on classic accounts of influence, namely social proof, authority, and scarcity ( Cialdini, 1984 ) , and on framing ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1981 ) . These accounts transfer to models. Across 126,000 126{,}000 conversations, prompts instantiating seven of Cialdini’s principles increased pooled partial-or-full compliance from 35.3 % 35.3\% to 51.3 % 51.3\% across three frontier models from different developers, a susceptibility the authors describe as parahuman ( Meincke et al., 2026 ) . That study concerns safety compliance rather than product choice, but authority, social proof, and scarcity each significantly increased compliance, showing that these cue families act on LLMs and not only on the humans they were formulated for. In decision tasks, LLMs likewise reproduce framing effects: in a synthetic admissions task, GPT-4 admitted 78.0 % 78.0\% of candidates under a reject-framed prompt versus 37.5 % 37.5\% under an admit-framed prompt, a difference of 40.5 40.5 percentage points ( Echterhoff et al., 2024 ) . Price has so far entered this literature as an outcome of cue-driven interaction rather than as a common scale for cue strength. For example, seller agents instructed to anchor obtained higher settlement prices in simulated bargaining ( Takenami et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Preference elicitation and price-denominated measurement.
sections.text: Random-utility and discrete-choice models provide the classical foundation for inferring preferences from observed choices ( McFadden, 1974 ) , including willingness-to-pay measures based on trade-offs with price ( Train, 2009 ) . Treating models as simulated economic agents that can be endowed with information, resources, and preferences has an established precedent ( Horton et al., 2023 ) , and price-denominated quantities can be recovered from them: WTP elicited from GPT-3 can be of realistic magnitude relative to human estimates ( Brand et al., 2023 ) , and Reusens et al. infer an LLM’s WTP for travel attributes and compare it to human estimates ( Reusens et al., 2026b ) . In concurrent work, Chu and Hou map an authority cue’s breakthrough rate to an equivalent rating gain, percentage price discount, or review-count multiplier ( Chu and Hou, 2026 ) . This is the closest price-denominated measure we are aware of. There, however, cue and price are evaluated in separate experiments, and the price equivalent is obtained by linearly interpolating a five-level price grid rather than by letting price and cue compete within the same trial. We instead vary price against the cue directly and read the parity crossing per cue and product pair, with position and cue target counterbalanced. We treat the resulting quantity as a prompt-conditional price equivalent rather than economic willingness to pay.

sections.heading: Measurement confounds and prompt sensitivity.
sections.text: Because our estimate is itself read from a prompt, we connect to work on LLM sensitivity to option order and to semantically irrelevant prompt features ( Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Sclar et al., 2024 ) , and to the broader use of LLMs as evaluators ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . The primacy we document is not unique to our stimuli: similar early-option preferences arise in a separately constructed, position-counterbalanced admissions benchmark ( Echterhoff et al., 2024 ) , and preference-manipulation attacks succeed more often when their wording overlaps with the user’s request ( Nestaas et al., 2024 ) . Two findings bear directly on reading a price equivalent off a prompt. Demand curves elicited from GPT-3 are broadly downward-sloping but generally not monotone in price ( Brand et al., 2023 ) . In blinded LLM simulations, varying price across otherwise comparable prompts can systematically alter the model’s implicit assumptions about unspecified pre-treatment characteristics and competing-product prices, which violates unconfoundedness ( Gui and Toubia, 2025 ) . We address both in Section 3 : position and cue target are counterbalanced within every cell (Section 3.2 ), and we read PE as a prompt-conditional threshold rather than a structural preference parameter (Section 3.1 ).

sections.heading: 3. Method
sections.text: We frame PE auditing as a reusable auditing protocol with three components: a counterbalanced, position-controlled price sweep that yields the price-equivalent (Section 3.1 ); a cue-free price-sensitivity control that calibrates cross-model comparison (Section 4.4 , Appendix E ); and a primacy diagnostic that guards choice-based readings (Section 3.2 , Section 4.5 ). The protocol applies unchanged to any seller-controlled intervention, model, or category; we instantiate it here on marketing cues across two categories and seven models (Table 1 ).

sections.heading: 3.1. Task, price-equivalent, and estimation
sections.text: A pair is two products matched on price, star rating, rating count, and specifications. One product carries a cue and the other does not. In a two-alternative forced choice, we first record P ⁡ ( choose cued ) P(\text{choose cued}) at equal price. We then raise the cued product’s price step by step, so that it costs a fixed percentage more than its otherwise identical counterpart. This premium runs across eight levels from 0 0 to 26 % 26\% ( 0 0 , 2 2 , 4 4 , 6 6 , 8 8 , 12 12 , 18 18 , and 26 % 26\% ) and is spaced more finely near zero, where most crossings fall. The 26 % 26\% ceiling is an empirical bracket, not a fixed constant. It sits above the largest price-equivalents we observe (the strongest cues cross near 13 13 – 22 % 22\% ), so the crossing falls inside the window for all but a few cues. We report those few as right-censored lower bounds ( † \dagger ). Premia beyond 26 % 26\% would add no crossing information, because by then even the strongest cue is almost always abandoned. The cue’s price-equivalent (PE) is the premium g ∗ g^{\ast} at which the cued product’s selection share falls to one half ( P = 0.5 P{=}0.5 ): how much more expensive the cued product may be before the agent abandons it, reported in percent of base price. Interpretation. A stronger willingness-to-pay reading would require a specified user, a budget constraint, and a utility model with a truth-inducing payoff, as in discrete-choice WTP estimation ( Reusens et al., 2026b ) . Our measure requires only that the agent trades price against the cue when it forms its recommendation. We vary price within a single trial across two fully specified, visible product cards. The reference product’s price is displayed and held constant, so the swept gap is the only quantity that moves. This avoids the between-prompt channel by which price variation can silently shift unspecified covariates in blinded LLM simulations ( Gui and Toubia, 2025 ) . It does not rule out that a model reads price itself as a quality signal. We treat this as a matter of interpretation rather than a design confound.

sections.heading: 3.2. Position control
sections.text: Agents over-select the first-presented option (Section 4.5 ), which near the parity crossing can bias PE. Within every (pair, price-point) cell we therefore counterbalance both position (the cued product is first in exactly half of trials) and cue target (the cue sits on product A and B equally often), with six calls in each of the four target–position states per cell, ruling out slot- and product-identity confounds.

sections.heading: 3.3. Experimental setup: cues, stimuli, models, and protocol
sections.text: Cues. Cues are single sentences appended to a product’s neutral description. Price, rating, and specifications stay untouched, so a cue competes only through its wording. We draw on several persuasion families. Social proof comes in four intensities, which serve as a dose-response calibration. Scarcity and authority enter as single sentences. Framing pairs hold information constant and vary only its form (percentage vs. fraction, a rescaled rating, and a gain/loss framing), so any premium reflects form rather than content. Three kinds of controls complete the set. Neutral and vacuous sentences test content-free additions. In a length control, a cue competes against a neutral sentence of matched length, which separates content from the mere presence of an added sentence. In a presence control, that neutral sentence competes against a second neutral sentence and should command no premium. Table 2 shows the exact sentences of the core cues. To study composition, we also measure one pre-specified sub-ceiling cue per family (social proof, authority, scarcity), singly and combined (Section 4.3 ). Stimuli. Stimuli are matched product pairs in two categories: six headphone pairs ($59.99–$199.99) and six coffee-machine pairs ($49.99–$299.99). Each neutral description was checked for persuasive content by an LLM judge on nine persuasion dimensions (headphones) and by a manual read of all pairs (Appendix N ). Models. We audit eight LLMs from four providers, each as a strong/weak pair: GPT-4o / GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet / Haiku, Nova Pro / Micro, and Llama-3.3-70B / 3.1-8B. GPT-4o is the reference model on which the full condition set runs. Two exclusions define the working sets used throughout. Nova Pro is dropped for a high non-response rate, which leaves the seven models of the main dataset over which we report aggregate figures (e.g. the headline trial count). The position-driven Llama-3.1-8B is additionally excluded from cross-model claims , which leaves the six task-engaged models those claims rest on. We additionally audit Jev , a decision-native model that returns a choice probability rather than text, with the same protocol (Section 4.7 ). Protocol. Each trial presents two product cards. Each card lists name, price, star rating, rating count, and description, and the cue is appended to the cued card’s description. A neutral instruction asks for a single option label: “A customer wants to buy {category}. Based on the two options shown, which would you recommend? Reply with only ‘Left’ or ‘Right’.” We parse the label by first-mentioned word match and treat unparsable replies as non-responses. We sample at temperature 0.7 0.7 with N = 24 N{=}24 repetitions per (pair, price point). One condition is therefore 6 × 8 × 24 = 1152 6\times 8\times 24=1152 trials, and the full audit totals 113,472 113{,}472 trials. Because the estimate is read from a prompt, we re-measure a cue subset under four semantically equivalent task paraphrases (Appendix J ). Exact wordings and model identifiers are in Appendix A , and the neutrality rubric is in Appendix N . All prompts, seeds, analysis code, and per-trial logs are available at https://github.com/Flexxbo/price-equivalent-auditing (Appendix O ).

sections.heading: 3.4. PE auditing in practice
sections.text: The protocol is meant to be re-run on new interventions, models, and categories, so we state the five operating rules our own results force. (1) Counterbalance position and cue target within every (pair, price-point) cell (Section 3.2 ). A first-option lean of the size we document (Section 4.5 ) otherwise leaks into the estimate, and the pooled value is the crossing of the averaged curves, not the mean of the per-order crossings. (2) Read the equal-price base rate as a two-sided validity gate. A rate near 0.5 0.5 on every cue signals a model that does not engage the task, and we exclude such a model from cross-model claims (Llama-3.1-8B, Section 4.4 ). For an engaged model, a rate near 0.5 0.5 on a single cue means that cue has no detectable pull (PE ≈ 0 \approx 0 ). A rate of exactly 1.00 1.00 signals an axis with no resolution left, where the cue’s pull is unidentified rather than high (authority on three models, Section 4.4 ). The gate fails at both ends. (3) Always run the cue-free price-only control alongside the sweep. PE combines cue pull with price sensitivity (under the single-index model of Appendix B it is exactly their ratio), so a raw magnitude is uninterpretable on its own, and a cross-model comparison of raw PE compares two things at once (Appendix E ). (4) Make censoring explicit. A cue dispreferred at equal price is floor-censored ( ‡ \ddagger ); a curve that never crosses within the sweep is right-censored ( † \dagger ). A censored cell is a bound, not a value, and must not enter a ranking as one (Section 3.1 ). (5) Read PE as ordinal-to-interval. Rankings and coarse magnitude bands survive task rephrasing and re-sampling; exact percentages drift by a few points across phrasings and vary widely across product pairs (Section 4.6 , Appendix F and Appendix J ).

sections.heading: 4. Results
sections.text: Unless noted, results are on the reference model (GPT-4o), position-controlled, with the model-free estimator and pair-clustered bootstrap 95 % 95\% CIs.

sections.heading: 4.1. A cue’s price, and why a choice rate under-resolves it
sections.text: At equal price the agent chose the strong social-proof product in 100 % 100\% of trials ( 144 / 144 144/144 ), and kept choosing it well into the positive-premium range. Its price-equivalent is ≈ 13 % \approx 13\% ( ≈ $ 17 \approx\$17 on a $130 item): the model-free estimator gives 12.9 % 12.9\% (CI [ 10.9 , 17.1 ] [10.9,17.1] ). An equal-price choice rate saturates, so a single-point audit cannot separate cues that a price axis resolves. A strong social-proof cue and a neutral factual sentence are each chosen in ≈ 100 % \approx 100\% of trials at equal price, so they are indistinguishable at the ceiling. The price sweep, however, separates them cleanly. The neutral sentence is abandoned almost immediately ( ≈ 2 % \approx 2\% premium), while social proof holds to ≈ 13 % \approx 13\% . A single equal-price rate loses this sixfold difference (Figure 2 ). The resolving power comes from the price intervention, not from PE per se: any audit that adds a common cardinal axis escapes the ceiling, whereas a single equal-price rate cannot. This divergence between choice and price echoes a long-documented human dissociation between choice and valuation, in which the two elicitations weight attributes differently and can even reverse ( Lichtenstein and Slovic, 1971 ; Tversky et al., 1988 ) . A price axis thus recovers a valuation signal that a choice-rate audit discards. The agents’ priced profile is nonetheless not a copy of the human one. Figure 2. Both cues win ≈ 100 % \approx 100\% at equal price; the sweep separates them (crossings at ≈ 2 % \approx 2\% and ≈ 13 % \approx 13\% ). Two curves of P(choose cued) versus price premium (0–26\%): both start near 1.0 at equal price; the neutral sentence crosses 0.5 near 2\% and strong social proof near 13\%. Across the battery the failure is not only one of resolution. Figure 3 plots every cue condition in two coordinates: the equal-price choice rate a conventional audit would report, and the price-equivalent. Six conditions sit at a base rate of 0.95 0.95 or above and are thus indistinguishable on the conventional axis. Priced, they span nearly 20 20 percentage points, from 1.6 % 1.6\% to 21.4 % 21.4\% . In the notation of Section 3.1 , these conditions share S Q ​ ( 0 ) ≥ 0.95 S_{Q}(0)\geq 0.95 , yet their price-equivalents PE Q \mathrm{PE}_{Q} differ by an order of magnitude: equal selection share at g = 0 g{=}0 , very different price. More sharply, the two axes disagree on order. Scarcity is chosen more often at equal price ( 0.95 0.95 ) than a gain/loss framing ( 0.72 0.72 ), yet its premium is fourteen times smaller ( 1.6 % 1.6\% vs. 22.3 % 22.3\% , disjoint intervals). A choice-rate audit therefore ranks the two the wrong way round. 2 2 2 The gain/loss condition is two-sided: both cards carry a matched form of the same fact, so its base rate reflects a choice between two framings rather than a cue against nothing. The ordering against scarcity is unaffected. This is not a precision problem that more trials would fix. The two quantities measure different things: how often a cue wins when price is tied, and how much price it can absorb. A cue can be broad and shallow (scarcity) or narrow and deep (gain/loss framing). Only the price a cue can absorb is what a seller can convert into money.

sections.heading: 4.2. Construct validity and a selective susceptibility profile
sections.text: A social-proof series of increasing intensity yields a monotonically rising, sharply nonlinear price-equivalent ( 0.7 < 1.3 < 12.9 < 21.4 % 0.7<1.3<12.9<21.4\% ). Weak and moderate claims sit near zero, and the premium switches on only at the strong claim. This is evidence that the instrument tracks persuasive strength. The steps are separated in the price metric, not merely ordered by point estimates: the weak, moderate, and strong social-proof intervals do not overlap on headphones (Appendix C ). The levels co-vary wording, customer count, and superlatives, so the series is an intensity gradient as a seller would write it, not a single-factor dose. Priced on one scale (Table 3 ), the battery is selective . Authority commands ≈ 19.8 % \approx 19.8\% , comparable to the strongest social-proof cue, and gain/loss framing ≈ 22 % \approx 22\% , whereas scarcity and number-preserving reformatting sit near the floor. A length-matched control ( ≈ 10.6 % \approx 10.6\% ) confirms that the premium comes from the sentence’s meaning , not from its length or mere presence (the cue-free price-only baseline is in Appendix E ). Scatter of the cue conditions on two axes: equal-price choice rate on the horizontal axis and price-equivalent on the vertical. Scarcity is the sharpest case of the thesis. An equal-price choice rate would call it strong, since the agent even prefers the scarcity-marked product at equal price. Yet it commands a price-equivalent of only 1.6 % 1.6\% (CI [ 1.4 , 1.9 ] [1.4,1.9] ), below 3 % 3\% , the level we treat as the instrument’s practical resolution. We read it as a small positive price-equivalent below our resolution. This departs from scarcity’s potency on human shoppers (a contrast with the persuasion literature, not a measured human baseline, and tested in a single formulation). Framing shows a clean dissociation. The agent is indifferent to number-preserving reformatting (a rescaled rating and a percent-vs-fraction restatement, both ≈ 0 % \approx 0\% ), yet it is strongly swayed by a gain/loss framing of the same fact ( ≈ 22 % \approx 22\% ). sections.heading: 4.3. Composition and generalization
sections.text: Re-running the battery on a second product category, coffee machines, reproduces the whole pattern. The dose-response, the gain/loss framing, the length and presence controls, the inert scarcity cue, and the null number-preserving framings all track their headphone values (Table 3 ). Authority also replicates ( ≈ 21.6 % \approx 21.6\% ) once its wording is made domain-appropriate. This exposes a further selectivity. The same authority sentence naming an irrelevant domain (“recommended by audio experts” on a coffee machine) is nearly inert ( ≈ 1.9 % \approx 1.9\% ), whereas a domain-matched version commands the full ≈ 22 % \approx 22\% . The agent thus responds to the relevance of an authority claim, not to the mere presence of an authoritative-sounding sentence. We test composition with a length-matched 2 3 2^{3} factorial. Three cross-family cues (social proof, authority, scarcity) are each present or absent in a fixed slot that otherwise holds a neutral filler. Sentence count is therefore constant, and the length/presence confound cancels in every interaction contrast (Appendix H ). Across six product pairs, no interaction is detectable, neither pairwise nor three-way. This holds on the log-odds scale (Firth-penalised ( Firth, 1993 ) , no term survives Holm correction ( Holm, 1979 ) ) and on the price scale (contrasts within a few points, all CIs spanning zero). Combined influence is thus consistent with additivity : an auditor could approximate a combination from single-cue measurements rather than testing every one. With only six clusters, our intervals still admit moderate interactions ( Cameron and Miller, 2015 ) .

Across these six, the social-proof series keeps its step pattern: the weak and moderate tiers stay at or below 4 % 4\% , and at least one strong tier lies clearly above them (Table 4 ). Scarcity commands at most 2 % 2\% on any model. Yet at equal price, GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini prefer the scarcity-marked product (base rates 0.95 0.95 and 0.88 0.88 ), whereas Claude Sonnet finds it aversive ( 0.19 0.19 , PE at most 0 0 ). This is the sharpest departure from classic persuasion accounts. Raw authority ( 1.6 1.6 – 19.8 % 19.8\% ) and gain/loss PEs ( 0 0 – 22.3 % 22.3\% , beyond 110 % 110\% on Nova Micro) look wildly model-specific. A PE, however, combines a cue’s pull with the model’s price sensitivity, and price sensitivity itself varies sharply. A model that barely reacts to price therefore records a large PE even for a modest pull. At + 10 % +10\% , GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, and Llama-3.3-70B almost never keep the pricier of two identical products, whereas Nova Micro does so about half the time (column p ↑ p_{\uparrow} ; Appendix E ). Read against the equal-price rates (Appendix E ), authority is broadly attractive on every task-engaged model ( 0.75 0.75 – 1.00 1.00 ). Claude Sonnet’s small authority PE ( 1.6 % 1.6\% ) thus reflects a steep price response, not an unmoved model. Gain/loss, by contrast, differs already at equal price , from immune (Llama-3.3-70B, 0.50 0.50 ) to strong (Nova Micro, 0.97 0.97 ). Nova Micro keeps choosing the cued product at more than double the price (an extended sweep to + 110 % +110\% ). Its PE is therefore not identified, and its apparent susceptibility is price-insensitivity. We report such models observationally rather than ranking a censored number. The upshot is that a cross-model audit should not be presumed to transfer, and raw PE must be read alongside price sensitivity, not as cue strength.

sections.heading: 4.5. Position: a confound to control, and a priced, platform-owned channel
sections.text: The agent disproportionately selects the first-presented option. Across the battery, it chooses the first option in 56.3 % 56.3\% of trials ( n = 14,976 n=14{,}976 ), rising to ≈ 65 % \approx 65\% in low-signal conditions (one-sided cues with a PE below 3 % 3\% ). Counterbalancing removes this lean from the pooled estimate, and a price × \times position test finds no distortion (Appendix D ). The bias nonetheless matters in itself. Any method that reads preferences off agent choices, including LLM-as-judge evaluation, must control option order or risk reporting position as preference. Under vision the bias becomes near-deterministic, which prevents identifying an image cue’s PE (Appendix M ). Counterbalancing does not mean averaging the two crossings. The pooled PE is the crossing of the averaged position-specific curves, which in general differs from the mean of their crossings. For scarcity, the slot-specific crossings are 6.1 % 6.1\% and 0.9 % 0.9\% (mean 3.5 % 3.5\% ), while the pooled PE is 1.6 % 1.6\% (Table 5 ). The policy-level PE is therefore a balanced-order summary, not a position-free cue strength. Likewise, a pooled share of one half is not indifference, since an agent that always picks the first-listed product also yields it (Appendix B ). Table 5. We read the cue-free price-only control per position. At equal price, the first slot sits at the choice-rate ceiling on every model, yet its price is gated by price sensitivity exactly as PE is. It is worth at most 3.2 % 3.2\% on the price-sensitive models, 14.0 % 14.0\% on GPT-4o mini, and beyond 80 % 80\% on the price-blind Nova Micro and Llama-3.1-8B (Appendix D ). An unchanged sweep thus also prices a non-linguistic intervention (Contribution 1).

sections.heading: 4.6. How precisely to read PE
sections.text: Holding a product’s facts and cues fixed, twelve truthful rewrites of one full description (strong social proof and scarcity woven in, LLM-generated) move GPT-4o’s PE from 2.3 % 2.3\% to 8.0 % 8.0\% (disjoint intervals, single pair, N = 30 N{=}30 per price point, logistic estimator). Wording is thus a real lever, but several times smaller than the choice of cue ( 0.7 0.7 – 21.4 % 21.4\% ). Two robustness views bound the precision. Under four semantically equivalent task phrasings, the social-proof ordering holds throughout. Strong social proof and gain/loss, however, exchange rank under one phrasing, and strong-cue premia drift by up to ≈ 8 \approx 8 points (Appendix J ). Within a condition, the six pair-level estimates for strong social proof range from 10.0 % 10.0\% to beyond 26 % 26\% around a pooled 12.9 % 12.9\% (Appendix F ). PE is therefore ordinal-to-interval: rankings and coarse bands are trustworthy, exact percentages are not.

sections.heading: PE-guided cue selection.
sections.text: On five headphone pairs, we score nine cues (three families × \times three intensities) by PE, freeze the top-scoring cue, and re-measure it out of sample. It commands + 13.3 +13.3 points more PE than the mean of the nine ( 95 % 95\% CI [ 8.7 , 17.8 ] [8.7,17.8] , Appendix I ). The saturated equal-price rate cannot make this choice. The search is deliberately simple, because the contribution is the objective, not the optimizer.

sections.heading: 4.7. Seller influence in a native decision model
sections.text: To test whether the hidden price is an artifact of text generation, we ran the full GPT-4o battery on Jev (TypeSafe AI) ( Almeida, 2026 ) , a decision-native model that returns a choice with a probability for each option. Jev received the chat models’ prompt verbatim, counterbalanced as in Section 3.2 ( 24 24 queries per pair and price point, 49,824 49{,}824 queries, none failed). We apply the paper’s estimator to its argmax choice (full results in Appendix K ).

sections.heading: The ceiling replicates, but the profile does not.
sections.text: Four cues (strong, very strong, and length-matched social proof, and authority) are chosen in every equal-price trial in both categories. Priced, they nevertheless span 1.5 1.5 – 16.6 % 16.6\% (headphones) and 1.2 1.2 – 19.6 % 19.6\% (coffee machines). The under-resolution of the equal-price rate is thus not specific to text-generating agents. Jev’s priced profile, however, is its own (Table 4 ). Social proof switches on only at the very strong claim ( 15.4 % 15.4\% ), authority is worth little ( 1.5 % 1.5\% against 19.8 % 19.8\% for GPT-4o), and gain/loss framing is worth nothing. Relevance, by contrast, matters sharply: the off-domain “audio experts” sentence on a coffee machine is never chosen at equal price ( 0 0 of 144 144 trials). Jev is as price-sensitive as GPT-4o ( 0 0 of 144 144 cue-free trials keep the pricier product at + 10 % +10\% ), so these differences are not price-blindness. Where no cue separates the cards, Jev picks the first-listed one (first slot in 60.1 % 60.1\% of battery trials, against 56.3 % 56.3\% for GPT-4o). Cue effects are also realized mostly in the first slot, so its pooled values summarize strongly slot-dependent behavior.

sections.heading: Cautions and scope.
sections.text: Jev’s prices depend on its input format. Passing the cards as a structured object raised strong social proof from 2.0 2.0 to 10.8 % 10.8\% . In addition, the filler sentence of its length-matched control is itself dispreferred, so that control does not transfer (Appendix K ). Under four task phrasings the cue ranking is stable, but the strong cues drift more than for GPT-4o (Appendix J ). To our knowledge, this is the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model. We do not attribute its differences to training or architecture, nor do we equate its stated probabilities with choice frequencies.

sections.heading: 5. Discussion
sections.text: Three threads run through these results. First, expressing a cue’s effect in price units makes its stakes legible. A cue that offsets a substantial premium is a buyer-invisible price shift, and putting heterogeneous cues in one monetary unit is what lets one compare them and act on them, whether the goal is to audit and govern agent-facing content or to optimize it. Second, the agents’ susceptibility is selective and does not mirror the profile that classic persuasion accounts would predict. Because it is cue-specific rather than blanket credulity, anyone reasoning about these agents must measure which cues actually move a given model rather than assume the textbook human-bias catalogue. And since cross-model magnitudes conflate cue pull with price sensitivity, an audit must not be extrapolated from one model to another. Third, primacy bias is a first-order property of agentic choice, not a nuisance to average away. Where content gives the agent little to go on, it falls back on “take the first one.” This is a concrete caution for the fast-growing practice of reading preferences off LLM choices.

sections.heading: Outlook: PE as a design objective.
sections.text: Because PE expresses influence in price units, it becomes usable as an objective in either direction, subject to the dual-use precautions of Section 7 . On the seller side, PE-guided cue selection is a demonstrated lever: the top-scoring of nine cues carries + 13.3 +13.3 percentage points more PE than the mean of the nine out of sample (Section 4.6 ). Combining cues, by contrast, is consistent with additivity (Section 4.3 , Appendix H ): no interaction between cues was detectable, so combined influence can be approximated from single-cue measurements.

sections.heading: 6. Limitations
sections.text: The audit is a deliberately controlled instrument, a synthetic two-alternative forced choice. It therefore measures susceptibility under clean conditions rather than predicting behaviour in a live shopping environment, where cues compete with search, reviews, and multi-step navigation. Our “non-human” characterization is a contrast with the human-persuasion literature , not a matched human baseline in our task. Each construct in the main battery is also tested in a single formulation, in particular one scarcity sentence. The low scarcity price-equivalent should therefore be read as low for this formulation, not as immunity to the construct. A price-equivalent combines a cue’s pull with the model’s price sensitivity, so cross-model magnitudes conflate the two. Models that do not respond to price even at large premiums have unidentified price-equivalents and are reported observationally, and several cues are censored at the top of the sweep (their true premia are lower bounds). The composition test covers one model and one cue per family.

sections.heading: Effective sample size and generalization.
sections.text: The headline trial count gives high precision with respect to each model’s stochastic sampling within a condition. The trials are, however, not independent product-level observations, because each condition repeats only six product pairs. Evidence therefore generalizes to different degrees along different axes. Two categories give initial cross-category evidence, but both are consumer-electronics durable goods, so generalization to structurally different domains (e.g., services such as travel or lodging) is untested. Four prompt paraphrases give limited robustness across task wording (the social-proof intensity ordering is preserved, while absolute magnitudes drift a few points). Generalization to new products is limited by six pairs per category. Finally, the audited models are a diverse convenience sample rather than a random draw, so claims hold for these models, not for “LLMs” in general. With only six pair-clusters, our confidence intervals may understate broader product-level uncertainty. We therefore report per-pair estimates and leave-one-pair-out sensitivity (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 7. Broader Impact and Dual Use
sections.text: Like any characterization of a susceptibility, a monetary measure of how much cues move agents is dual-use. It supports scrutiny and governance, since developers, platforms, and auditors can detect which cues move which models and monitor drift. Equally, it supports content optimization for agent-mediated markets ( generative engine optimization , GEO). We state this dual-use character openly rather than claiming a single intended use. The line we draw is truthfulness , not the direction of use. Every cue here is a single, factually plausible sentence stipulated true of the product. We neither fabricate false claims nor optimize toward deception, and we stress that “plausible” is not “verified.” Enforcing genuine factuality in a deployed system would require ground-truth checks that we do not provide. As a matter of responsible release, we make available per-trial logs, stimuli, prompts, and analysis code, but not a turnkey library of optimized manipulative descriptions, and we encourage the same practice for follow-up work. The study uses no human subjects and no personal data.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced price-equivalent auditing, which expresses a marketing cue’s effect on an LLM shopping agent as the price premium it can offset, turning qualitative susceptibility into a comparable monetary quantity. On this scale, the agents’ response is selective, not a simple copy of the human profile, and partly shared across models. Because raw magnitudes must be read alongside price sensitivity rather than as cue strength, the response resists a single cross-model ranking. It is further shaped by a strong primacy bias that any choice-based evaluation must control. Expressing influence in price units gives a common basis for studying, and acting on, how content moves agents in agent-mediated markets. Acknowledgements. sections.text: We audit eight LLMs from four providers (GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini, OpenAI; Claude Sonnet and Haiku, Anthropic; Nova Pro and Micro, Amazon; Llama-3.3-70B and 3.1-8B, Meta), each sampled at temperature 0.7 0.7 . The other models run a core cue subset for the cross-model comparison. Exact model identifiers and collection dates are in Table 25 .

sections.heading: Text prompt.
sections.text: Every trial combines a fixed system prompt with a user prompt. The user prompt names the product subcategory (inserted verbatim from the product file, e.g. “over-ear wireless ANC”), shows two option cards labelled by slot, and asks for a single label. Each card lists name, price, star rating with rating count, and description. A cue is one sentence appended to the cued product’s description. sections.text: The four task phrasings (Table 6 ) share the product cards and the closing “Reply with only ‘Left’ or ‘Right’.” instruction. Only the intro line and the question change. sections.heading: Cue wordings.
sections.text: Table 7 lists every cue sentence. In the notation of Section 3.1 , c 1 c_{1} is appended to the cued product and c 0 c_{0} to the comparator. For most conditions the comparator carries no sentence. Framing conditions place the matched alternative form on the comparator, and the length and presence controls place a neutral sentence there. sections.text: The two product cards are rendered to one screenshot; the user prompt is “A customer wants to buy {category}. The image shows two options side by side, a Left option and a Right option. Based on what is shown, which would you recommend? Reply with only ‘Left’ or ‘Right’.”

sections.heading: Image generation & text screening.
sections.text: Standard images: “Professional e-commerce catalog photo of a plain, unbranded pair of {subcategory} … pure-white seamless background … no text, letters, numbers, logos, brand names, labels, or watermarks.” Optimized images are produced by editing the standard image (“change only the scene … keep the product pixel-identical”), with the same no-text constraints. sections.heading: Formal definition and properties.
sections.text: We restate the estimand of Section 3.1 and record its basic properties. Estimand. Write h = c 1 : c 0 h=c_{1}\!:\!c_{0} for the cue contrast and S Q ​ ( g ) ≡ S Q ​ ( g ∣ h , M , π ) S_{Q}(g)\equiv S_{Q}(g\mid h,M,\pi) for the policy-averaged selection share of the c 1 c_{1} -bearing product at proportional premium g g . Then PE Q ​ ( h ) = inf { g : S Q ​ ( g ) ≤ 1 2 } . \mathrm{PE}_{Q}(h)=\inf\{\,g:S_{Q}(g)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\,\}. The threshold 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} follows from role-swap symmetry rather than an identical-products assumption: when the cue is unobservable at g = 0 g{=}0 the no-cue baseline share is b Q = S Q ( 0 ∣ c 0 : c 0 ) = 1 2 b_{Q}=S_{Q}(0\mid c_{0}\!:\!c_{0})=\tfrac{1}{2} under our balanced policy, and the general estimand PE Q base ​ ( h ) = inf { g : S Q ​ ( g ) ≤ b Q } \mathrm{PE}^{\mathrm{base}}_{Q}(h)=\inf\{g:S_{Q}(g)\leq b_{Q}\} then coincides with it. Existence and uniqueness. If S Q S_{Q} is weakly decreasing and there are premia g L < g U g_{L}<g_{U} with S Q ​ ( g L ) > 1 2 ≥ S Q ​ ( g U ) S_{Q}(g_{L})>\tfrac{1}{2}\geq S_{Q}(g_{U}) , a crossing g ∗ ∈ [ g L , g U ] g^{\ast}\in[g_{L},g_{U}] exists; if S Q S_{Q} is strictly decreasing around it, g ∗ g^{\ast} is unique. If S Q S_{Q} rests at 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} over an interval, the parity set is that interval; in our data this occurs only for the excluded, position-driven Llama-3.1-8B (Appendix G ). A pre-specified single-downward-crossing rule (below) resolves sampling non-monotonicity. Censoring. On the swept support [ 0 , g max ] [0,g_{\max}] : if S Q ​ ( g max ) > 1 2 S_{Q}(g_{\max})>\tfrac{1}{2} the crossing is right-censored and we report a lower bound PE Q > g max \mathrm{PE}_{Q}>g_{\max} ( † \dagger ); if S Q ​ ( 0 ) ≤ 1 2 S_{Q}(0)\leq\tfrac{1}{2} the cue is dispreferred at equal price, PE Q \mathrm{PE}_{Q} is left-censored (PE ≤ 0 {}\leq 0 , ‡ \ddagger ), and the equal-price base rate gives the identified sign. Sizing an aversive contrast would require a two-sided sweep.

sections.heading: Estimator.
sections.text: For a cue we sweep the price gap g g on the cued product and record the counterbalanced choice rate P ⁡ ( choose cued ) P(\text{choose cued}) at each g g ; the price-equivalent is the gap at which P P crosses 0.5 0.5 . The primary estimator is model-free: it interpolates the crossing of the two-order-averaged choice curve, making no parametric assumption about the curve’s shape and staying robust to the saturation cues produce. When the averaged curve is non-monotone it can in principle cross 0.5 0.5 more than once; we take the first downward crossing from the low-price end. This rule is fixed in the released code: on the finite grid the crossing is the first interval in which the empirical curve passes from ≥ 1 2 {\geq}\tfrac{1}{2} to strictly below 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} , so a grid point that sits exactly at 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} and is followed by a rebound is treated as sampling noise. One identified cell is affected (Claude Haiku, strong social proof: 9.8 % 9.8\% , which reads 6.0 % 6.0\% under the strict infimum). This is rarely at issue empirically: across all 84 84 swept curves (including the price-only controls and the excluded Nova Pro), 79 79 show a single 0.5 0.5 -crossing or none. The five exceptions are confined to Llama-3.1-8B, Nova Micro, and the excluded Nova Pro, whose curves hover within ± 5 \pm 5 percentage points of 0.5 0.5 (sampling noise, not genuine non-monotonicity), a caution consistent with reports that LLM demand curves need not be monotone in price ( Brand et al., 2023 ) . As a parametric cross-check we fit a position-controlled logistic, P = σ ( β 0 + β 1 g + β 2 1 [ cued first ] ) , PE = − ( β 0 + 1 2 β 2 ) / β 1 , P=\sigma\!\big(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}g+\beta_{2}\,\mathbf{1}[\text{cued first}]\big),\qquad\mathrm{PE}=-(\beta_{0}+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_{2})/\beta_{1}, read at the mean position indicator 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} ; an interaction variant relaxing the constant-position assumption is in Appendix D . Confidence intervals are pair-clustered bootstrap ( 2000 2000 resamples over the six product pairs). Because PE = pull / ( − β 1 ) \mathrm{PE}=\text{pull}/(-\beta_{1}) is a ratio of cue pull to price sensitivity, Appendix E separates the two.

sections.heading: A note on pooling.
sections.text: The price slope varies substantially across conditions— β 1 ≈ − 1.1 \beta_{1}\approx-1.1 per percentage point in the cue-free price-only control, versus ≈ − 0.3 \approx-0.3 under strong social proof and ≈ − 0.1 \approx-0.1 under gain/loss framing. A logistic pooled across conditions with a single price coefficient would therefore be misspecified, and an interaction term read from such a fit would absorb slope differences rather than measure interaction. The model-free estimator makes no such assumption, and the parametric cross-check is fitted per condition.

sections.heading: Pooled vs. product-level PE.
sections.text: The pooled PE Q \mathrm{PE}_{Q} is the crossing of the population curve S Q ​ ( g ) = 𝔼 X ∼ Q ​ [ s X ​ ( g ) ] S_{Q}(g)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[s_{X}(g)] , not the average of the per-pair crossings: in general PE Q ≠ 𝔼 X ∼ Q ​ [ PE X ] \mathrm{PE}_{Q}\neq\mathbb{E}_{X\sim Q}[\mathrm{PE}_{X}] , and likewise for the per-position crossings, because pairs with different slopes contribute differently to the root of the averaged curve. A pooled share of 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} can therefore arise with no pair (or position) at parity. We accordingly report the pooled value together with the distribution of per-pair estimates (Appendix F ) and the per-position crossings (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Random-utility reading.
sections.text: Under a single-index model S Q ​ ( g ) = F ⁡ ( δ h − λ h ​ g ) S_{Q}(g)=F(\delta_{h}-\lambda_{h}g) with F F strictly increasing, F ⁡ ( 0 ) = 1 2 F(0)=\tfrac{1}{2} , net cue advantage δ h \delta_{h} , and price sensitivity λ h > 0 \lambda_{h}>0 , the crossing is g ∗ = δ h / λ h g^{\ast}=\delta_{h}/\lambda_{h} —the “cue pull over price sensitivity” reading of PE = pull / ( − β 1 ) \mathrm{PE}=\text{pull}/(-\beta_{1}) above. This holds within a condition; a common-slope decomposition across cues needs λ h ≡ λ \lambda_{h}\equiv\lambda (no cue × \times price interaction), which the slope differences above rule out here. A willingness-to-pay reading needs more still (a budget, price as cost rather than quality, a specified user); absent these, PE is a descriptive content-vs-price exchange rate, not welfare or WTP.

sections.heading: Assumptions.
sections.text: The operational estimand rests on the following assumptions. A1 Stable audit environment: fixed model snapshot, prompt, decoding, and card template. A2 Explicit comparator: the comparator content c 0 c_{0} is part of the estimand. A3 Joint design control: the four ( T , R ) (T,R) cells carry weight 1 4 \tfrac{1}{4} , exactly balanced in our data. A4 Single crossing: S Q S_{Q} is weakly decreasing over the search domain. A5 Support: the price sweep brackets the crossing; otherwise a bound is reported. A6 Local smoothness: the curve is approximately linear between the two bracketing grid points. A7 Stable repeated sampling: no model drift during collection (Appendix O ). A8 Explicit population: the product distribution Q Q is part of the estimand. A9 Forced-choice scope: the threshold pertains to the stated two-option protocol. A10 Relative-price scale: PE is a proportional premium on the reference price. Where an assumption binds (saturation, censoring, non-monotonicity, cue × \times price interaction), we flag it in the main text.

sections.heading: Appendix D Position control: interaction robustness
sections.text: The parametric cross-check of Section 3.1 enters the order indicator additively , which assumes a constant first-option advantage. Because the first-option lean varies across the sweep (Section 4.5 ), the position effect may itself depend on the price gap, which an additive term cannot capture. As a specification check we refit the anchor strong-social-proof condition with a price × \times position interaction, P = σ ⁡ ( β 0 + β 1 ​ g + β 2 ​ 1 ​ [ cued first ] + β 3 ​ g ​ 1 ​ [ cued first ] ) , P=\sigma\!\big(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}g+\beta_{2}\,\mathbf{1}[\text{cued first}]+\beta_{3}\,g\,\mathbf{1}[\text{cued first}]\big), and read the position-neutral crossing at the mean indicator 1 2 \tfrac{1}{2} , PE = − ( β 0 + 1 2 β 2 ) / ( β 1 + 1 2 β 3 ) \mathrm{PE}=-(\beta_{0}+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_{2})/(\beta_{1}+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta_{3}) . Across the four highest-impact cues on GPT-4o the interaction is never identified: the coefficient β 3 \beta_{3} has a pair-clustered bootstrap 95 % 95\% CI spanning zero for every cue, and the position-neutral price-equivalent moves by at most ≈ 1 \approx 1 percentage point relative to the additive fit (Table 9 ). sections.heading: Position-specific crossings.
sections.text: As a direct, non-parametric complement we also estimate the price-equivalent separately for the two orders (Table 5 ). The cued-first crossing is uniformly higher than the cued-second crossing—position adds a real per-trial advantage—but the two are consistent: they preserve the cue ordering and bracket the counterbalanced pooled value. For weak cues this order dependence is large relative to the pooled value, so the policy-level PE should be read as a balanced-order summary rather than a position-free cue strength. The distinction between this pooled crossing and the arithmetic mean of the two separate crossings is drawn in Section 4.5 . (For the two-sided framing conditions, where both options carry a sentence, the per-order split is less clean and we rely on the pooled estimate.)

sections.heading: Appendix F Effective sample size: pair-level estimates and leave-one-pair-out
sections.text: Because each condition contains only six product pairs, the cluster bootstrap generalizes over six units, and a percentile interval on six clusters can understate uncertainty ( Cameron and Miller, 2015 , Sec. VI) . We therefore complement the intervals with two transparent robustness views.

sections.heading: Pair-level spread.
sections.text: For the strong social-proof cue the six per-pair price-equivalents are (GPT-4o, model-free, N = 24 N=24 per price point): In-ear ANC ($89.99) 10.2 10.2 ; On-ear ($79.99) 14.6 14.6 ; Over-ear ANC ($129.99) 10.0 10.0 ; Over-ear premium ($199.99) 19.1 19.1 ; Sport earbuds ($59.99) 11.2 11.2 ; Wired studio ($149.99) beyond 26 26 (no crossing); pooled 12.9 % 12.9\% —real product heterogeneity around a stable pooled value (the position-controlled per-pair estimate can inflate under near-separation, which the model-free estimator and bootstrap CIs guard against).

sections.heading: Leave-one-pair-out (scarcity).
sections.text: Dropping any single pair leaves scarcity’s pooled price-equivalent between 1.5 % 1.5\% and 1.7 % 1.7\% —below the 3 % 3\% resolution threshold (Section 4.2 ) for every hold-out—so the “small average positive, below resolution” reading does not hinge on any one pair (two individual pairs reach 4 % 4\% , but the pooled and leave-one-out estimates stay under 2 % 2\% ). These checks are more interpretable than a small-sample variance correction and make the six-cluster basis explicit; broadening product-level generalization would require more pairs, which we flag as the main design limitation rather than a reporting one. The per-pair spread ( 10 10 to over 26 % 26\% ) is genuine product heterogeneity, which the pooled estimand averages over by design.

sections.heading: Appendix H Cue-combination additivity
sections.text: We test whether cross-family cue effects combine additively with a length-matched 2 3 2^{3} factorial. Three families—social proof, authority, and scarcity—occupy three fixed slots; each slot carries either its cue or a fixed neutral filler, so every one of the eight conditions holds sentence count constant at three. Because the filler is fixed per slot, its contribution cancels exactly in every interaction contrast, removing the length/presence confound by construction . We measure all eight conditions on six product pairs (GPT-4o, model-free PE and a position-controlled logistic, a shared grid extended to + 60 % +60\% , N = 24 N=24 per point). Table 16 reports the four interaction terms on two scales: the model-free price-scale interaction contrast ( Δ \Delta PE, per condition—our primary readout) and a Firth-penalised factorial logistic (ceiling-robust cross-check) with a pair-cluster bootstrap CI. No term is significant after Holm correction on the log-odds scale, and every price-scale contrast is within a few points with a CI spanning zero: combined influence is consistent with additivity at our precision. With six clusters the intervals still admit moderate interactions ( Cameron and Miller, 2015 , Sec. VI) , so we read the result as “no detectable interaction” rather than exact additivity. Table 16. sections.heading: Appendix K Jev: full results
sections.text: This appendix collects the Jev details summarized in Section 4.7 . Table 21 gives Jev’s full battery in both categories with equal-price choice rates, pair-clustered intervals, and slot-specific crossings; Figure 5 splits the choice curves by slot.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Jev received the chat models’ prompt verbatim—the same product cards, cue sentences, prices, and Left/Right options, with the system prompt and question as its instruction— counterbalanced as in Section 3.2 , with 24 24 queries per (pair, price point) on a finer price grid; price-equivalents are computed on the paper’s grid points. We apply the paper’s estimator to Jev’s argmax choice; the crossings of its stated probability agree closely and are not equated with it.

sections.heading: Profile in detail.
sections.text: Jev’s social-proof series switches on only at the very strong claim ( 0.5 0.5 , 0.0 0.0 , 2.0 2.0 , and 15.4 % 15.4\% on headphones, against GPT-4o’s 0.7 0.7 , 1.3 1.3 , 12.9 12.9 , and 21.4 % 21.4\% ); authority is worth little ( 1.5 1.5 and 1.2 % 1.2\% against 19.8 19.8 and 21.6 % 21.6\% ), and gain/loss framing nothing. The off-domain sentence “recommended by audio experts” on a coffee machine is never chosen at equal price ( 0 0 of 144 144 trials), whereas GPT-4o treats it as nearly inert ( 1.9 % 1.9\% ). Number-preserving reformatting is not neutral either: Jev dislikes “4.8 out of 5” against “9.6 out of 10” (base rates 0.21 0.21 and 0.42 0.42 ).

sections.heading: Position.
sections.text: In the price-only control, for the vacuous claim, and for percent/fraction and gain/loss framing Jev chooses the first card in every equal-price trial and the second in none. Very strong social proof holds beyond 26 % 26\% when shown first but crosses at 4.2 4.2 and 1.8 % 1.8\% when shown second; for strong social proof the slot-specific crossings are 10.3 10.3 versus 1.2 % 1.2\% (headphones), against 16.2 16.2 versus 10.1 % 10.1\% for GPT-4o (Table 5 ). Jev’s pooled values are therefore balanced-order summaries of strongly slot-dependent behavior (Figure 5 ).

sections.heading: Two cautions.
sections.text: First, the length and presence controls do not transfer: the “neutral” identification-code sentence is itself dispreferred by Jev (presence control, base rates 0.32 0.32 and 0.17 0.17 ), so the length-matched social-proof condition ( 16.6 16.6 and 19.6 % 19.6\% ) exceeds social proof alone ( 2.0 2.0 and 1.6 % 1.6\% ) instead of isolating its content. Second, Jev’s prices depend on its input format: an earlier run that passed the same cards as a structured object with slot-named options gave strong social proof 10.8 % 10.8\% on headphones and more than 26 % 26\% on coffee machines, against 2.0 2.0 and 1.6 % 1.6\% with the chat prompt.

sections.heading: Robustness to phrasing.
sections.text: Under the four task phrasings of Appendix J (six cues, headphones, 12 12 queries per pair and price point; 20,736 20{,}736 queries), the unchanged phrasing reproduces the main run (strong social proof 1.8 1.8 vs. 2.0 % 2.0\% , very strong 15.4 15.4 vs. 15.4 % 15.4\% ). The cue ranking is identical under the three paraphrases and nearly so under the original, very strong social proof exceeds strong social proof in every phrasing, and gain/loss framing stays at zero throughout. Two things are less stable than for GPT-4o (Table 20 ): weak social proof outprices moderate social proof under every phrasing ( 0.4 0.4 – 1.0 1.0 vs. 0.0 0.0 – 0.6 % 0.6\% ), and the strong cues drift more ( 1.8 1.8 – 7.0 % 7.0\% for strong, 14.2 14.2 to beyond 26 % 26\% for very strong social proof, against 10.2 10.2 – 17.7 17.7 and 16.4 16.4 – 24.7 % 24.7\% for GPT-4o).

sections.heading: Appendix M The presentation (image) cue: full results
sections.text: The two product cards (image, name, price, rating, description) are rendered to a single side-by-side screenshot and shown to the vision model with the same forced-choice instruction; a position-free single-image probe additionally asks for a 1 1 – 10 10 “premium/appeal” rating. Under vision the primacy bias becomes near-deterministic: at equal price the agent chooses the first option in 100 % 100\% of trials, so P ⁡ ( choose cued ) P(\text{choose cued}) is 0.50 0.50 for every pair by construction, relaxing only as price diverges (Table 23 ); that it responds to price at all confirms it reads the rendered cards. In the perception probe the optimised image is rated slightly more premium than the standard image, so the manipulation is perceptible; yet its price-equivalent cannot be identified, because primacy saturates the response channel in the small-premium regime that matters for elicitation. This is a boundary case of our counterbalanced ( 50 / 50 50/50 ) policy estimand (Section 3.1 )—when option-order choice is near-deterministic, the policy average is pinned at 0.50 0.50 and PE is not identified—not evidence of a null; a position-free paradigm (single-product valuation, or an image-only 2AFC) is required to estimate an image premium. sections.heading: Appendix N Stimulus neutrality audit
sections.text: Within a pair, price, rating, rating count, and specifications are identical, and the two neutral descriptions are length-matched (word count within ± 15 % \pm 15\% ). For the headphone pairs, each description was rated 1 1 – 5 5 on nine persuasion dimensions (social proof, scarcity, authority, exclusivity, urgency, discount framing, storytelling, emotional language, comparative language) by an LLM judge (Claude Opus) instructed to score strictly, so that any hint of a cue scores ≥ 3 \geq 3 . A description is accepted only if it scores ≤ 2 \leq 2 on all nine, and every headphone description scored 1 1 on every dimension. In addition, the first author read all twelve pairs in both categories and checked them for persuasive wording (social proof, scarcity, authority, evaluative wording, superlatives, embedded price or rating) and for balanced wording between the two sides. All twelve pairs passed. After the audit, the judge rubric was extended by a tenth dimension (normative/eco valence), because the judge had passed a sustainability-coded sentence that nonetheless commanded a premium. This extension was not used to re-score the stimuli. Structural checks additionally enforce identical specifications, identical price and rating, and matched description length. The rubric, the judge scores, and the manual audit are released (Appendix O ).

sections.text: Sampling temperature 0.7 0.7 ; N = 24 N{=}24 trials per (pair, price-point) ( N = 12 N{=}12 for the robustness paraphrases); premium levels 0 0 , 2 2 , 4 4 , 6 6 , 8 8 , 12 12 , 18 18 , and 26 % 26\% , extended to 60 % 60\% for the additivity runs; bootstrap of 2000 2000 resamples clustered by product pair; fixed random seed; position and cue-target counterbalancing within each (pair, price-point) cell. Code, stimuli, prompts, and per-trial logs are available at https://github.com/Flexxbo/price-equivalent-auditing as a reusable implementation of the auditing protocol (Section 3 ), so the audit can be re-run on new interventions, models, and categories. Our fixed seed therefore pins only stimulus construction and counterbalancing, not model sampling; for closed APIs this does not guarantee identical outputs, so we release per-trial logs and report results as distributions over N N repeats rather than single deterministic outputs.

text: A Cue’s Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved.
