Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.25843v1 [cs.AI] 19 Oct 2026 A Cue’s Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers CCS: Computing methodologies Natural language processing CCS: Computing methodologies Machine learning CCS: Computing methodologies Multi-agent systems CCS: Applied computing Online shopping CCS: Information systems Recommender systems Felix Buecheler Affiliation: Adelaide University , Adelaide , Australia email: felix.buecheler@adelaide.edu.au , Gerardo Berbeglia Affiliation: Melbourne Business School , Melbourne , Australia and Mingyu Guo Affiliation: Adelaide University , Adelaide , Australia Abstract. Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user’s behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent’s choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product’s price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue’s price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 113{,}472 trials, seven models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev , which outputs a choice probability directly instead of generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark that reports each model’s cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents. Keywords: LLM agents, agentic commerce, marketing cues, persuasion, price-equivalent, evaluation, GEO 1. Introduction Large language models are moving from answering questions to acting , as shopping agents that browse, compare, and buy on a user’s behalf. When a model rather than a person makes the choice, a seller’s leverage shifts from persuading a human to steering an agent. Seller-controlled cues such as a “best-seller” claim, an endorsement, or a framed specification can tilt an agent’s recommendation. Such a cue acts like a hidden discount: it makes the agent more likely to choose the product, just as a lower price would, yet no price changes and the buyer never sees it (Figure 1 ). As agentic commerce scales, how much such content shifts an agent’s choice becomes an economically consequential quantity. It matters whether one audits and governs these agents or optimizes content for them, and comparing it across cues requires a common scale . Prior work establishes that LLM shopping agents are susceptible to such cues and that presentation can move them ( Cherep et al., 2026a ; Filandrianos et al., 2025 ; Cherep et al., 2026b ) . It mostly reports their effects as shifts in choice probability, however, and this scale can mislead exactly where it matters. Strong cues saturate the choice near 100 % 100\% and become indistinguishable, and a counterbalanced first-option bias averages to a 50 % 50\% rate that looks like indifference. What such rates leave out is the price that offsets a cue’s influence. Knowing that a cue “raises selection” says nothing about whether it is worth a few cents or a large fraction of the product’s price. We therefore treat a cue’s effect as a hidden price and measure it directly, rather than inferring it from matched response rates ( Chu and Hou, 2026 ) . In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product’s price until it is chosen only half the time. We call that premium the cue’s price-equivalent (PE): the price premium that just offsets the cue’s pull on the agent’s recommendation. Price-equivalent auditing turns qualitative susceptibility into a single monetary number and places text and framing cues on one comparable scale. Figure 1. Auditing a cue as a hidden price (schematic). Three-panel schematic of price-equivalent auditing: an agent prefers a cued product at equal price; a price sweep locates each sentence's price-equivalent; a cue and a neutral sentence are both chosen near 100\% of the time yet differ sixfold in price-equivalent. We price single-sentence cues that a seller can place in a listing. They include endorsements that carry information (authority, social proof, e.g. “chosen by over 10,000 customers”), scarcity claims (“only a few left in stock”), and number-preserving reframings of the same facts (gain/loss, rating rescaling, percent/fraction), and they draw on classic accounts of influence ( Cialdini, 1984 ) and framing ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1981 ) . We also price option order, a channel the platform rather than the seller controls. We use persuasion as a motivating umbrella. PE audits seller-controlled influence relative to price and does not by itself show that a cue induces an irrational bias. For information-bearing cues, PE captures the combined effect of information and presentation. For information-preserving framing, it isolates presentation. Both matter for auditing what a seller can change, even though they are interpreted differently. Contributions. (1) The price-equivalent, formally defined and audited. We define a cue’s price-equivalent as a money-denominated selection-parity threshold: the price premium at which the cued product’s selection share, averaged over a balanced presentation policy, falls to one half. We give a nonparametric definition with conditions for existence and censoring, and a single-index model in which the cue enters as an additive utility term. Around it we build a reusable, counterbalanced audit protocol with a cue-free price-sensitivity control and a primacy diagnostic. The protocol applies unchanged across cues, models, and categories, and it even prices a non-linguistic intervention that the platform controls: option order (Section 3 ). (2) What priced auditing reveals. Across 113,472 113{,}472 trials, seven models, and two categories, a price axis resolves what an equal-price choice rate cannot. Six cue conditions are each chosen in at least 95 % 95\% of trials and are thus indistinguishable at equal price, yet their price-equivalents range from 1.6 % 1.6\% to 21.4 % 21.4\% . The equal-price ranking can even invert: gain/loss framing commands one of the largest premiums but is chosen less often than scarcity. The resulting susceptibility profile is selective and model-specific, and it replicates in a second category. The same pricing turns the well-documented first-option (primacy) bias from a nuisance into a priced channel that the platform controls. Because this bias can look like indifference, it is a caution for any choice-based evaluation of agents, including LLM-as-judge (Section 4 ). (3) The first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model. We apply the instrument to Jev , a model that returns a choice probability directly instead of generating text. The equal-price ceiling and its resolution by price reappear, so they are not artifacts of text generation. Jev also shows a susceptibility profile of its own: it resists most cues but is moved by the strongest social-proof claims (Section 4.7 ). As a resource, we release the stimuli, prompts, seeds, per-trial logs, and code as a benchmark that others can run on new models and categories. 1 1 1 https://github.com/Flexxbo/price-equivalent-auditing It reports each model’s cue-price profile rather than a single score, because raw PE must be read alongside price sensitivity and therefore resists a single cross-model ranking (Section 4.4 ). 2. Related Work LLM agents in shopping and consumer choice. WebShop and VisualWebArena established web shopping as an agent-evaluation setting, but measure task completion and grounding rather than how seller-controlled content changes preferences ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Koh et al., 2024 ) . On a benchmark built from 31,865 31{,}865 real online-shopping sessions, prompt-only LLMs poorly predict users’ next actions, with the strongest baseline reaching 11.86 % 11.86\% accuracy, and tend to generate more purchases than the observed users ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . Recent conceptual work argues that classical consumer frameworks must evolve as LLM agents increasingly act on users’ behalf, which leaves the steerability of agent choices an open question ( Reusens et al., 2026a ) . That such choices can be steered is well documented. Closest to our setting, ABxLab manipulates prices, ratings, product order, and textual nudges across multiple LLM agents and finds large and predictable shifts in choice ( Cherep et al., 2026a ) . Bias Beware frames cognitive-bias cues as black-box attacks on recommender systems ( Filandrianos et al., 2025 ) , Visual Persuasion shows that image edits steer vision-language model choices ( Cherep et al., 2026b ) , and altering only an item’s title can raise its exposure in LLM-based recommenders while leaving overall recommendation performance largely unchanged ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . The incentive is not hypothetical. Crafted page content can make production search assistants promote one seller’s products and discredit competitors’, creating a prisoner’s-dilemma-like dynamic in which recommendation rates fall for all products as attacks proliferate ( Nestaas et al., 2024 ) . Optimising content for generative engines has already been formalised as Generative Engine Optimization ( Aggarwal et al., 2024 ) . Persuasion and behavioural bias in LLMs. The cues we study draw on classic accounts of influence, namely social proof, authority, and scarcity ( Cialdini, 1984 ) , and on framing ( Tversky and Kahneman, 1981 ) . These accounts transfer to models. Across 126,000 126{,}000 conversations, prompts instantiating seven of Cialdini’s principles increased pooled partial-or-full compliance from 35.3 % 35.3\% to 51.3 % 51.3\% across three frontier models from different developers, a susceptibility the authors describe as parahuman ( Meincke et al., 2026 ) . That study concerns safety compliance rather than product choice, but authority, social proof, and scarcity each significantly increased compliance, showing that these cue families act on LLMs and not only on the humans they were formulated for. In decision tasks, LLMs likewise reproduce framing effects: in a synthetic admissions task, GPT-4 admitted 78.0 % 78.0\% of candidates under a reject-framed prompt versus 37.5 % 37.5\% under an admit-framed prompt, a difference of 40.5 40.5 percentage points ( Echterhoff et al., 2024 ) . Price has so far entered this literature as an outcome of cue-driven interaction rather than as a common scale for cue strength. For example, seller agents instructed to anchor obtained higher settlement prices in simulated bargaining ( Takenami et al., 2025 ) . Preference elicitation and price-denominated measurement. Random-utility and discrete-choice models provide the classical foundation for inferring preferences from observed choices ( McFadden, 1974 ) , including willingness-to-pay measures based on trade-offs with price ( Train, 2009 ) . Treating models as simulated economic agents that can be endowed with information, resources, and preferences has an established precedent ( Horton et al., 2023 ) , and price-denominated quantities can be recovered from them: WTP elicited from GPT-3 can be of realistic magnitude relative to human estimates ( Brand et al., 2023 ) , and Reusens et al. infer an LLM’s WTP for travel attributes and compare it to human estimates ( Reusens et al., 2026b ) . In concurrent work, Chu and Hou map an authority cue’s breakthrough rate to an equivalent rating gain, percentage price discount, or review-count multiplier ( Chu and Hou, 2026 ) . This is the closest price-denominated measure we are aware of. There, however, cue and price are evaluated in separate experiments, and the price equivalent is obtained by linearly interpolating a five-level price grid rather than by letting price and cue compete within the same trial. We instead vary price against the cue directly and read the parity crossing per cue and product pair, with position and cue target counterbalanced. We treat the resulting quantity as a prompt-conditional price equivalent rather than economic willingness to pay. Measurement confounds and prompt sensitivity. Because our estimate is itself read from a prompt, we connect to work on LLM sensitivity to option order and to semantically irrelevant prompt features ( Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Sclar et al., 2024 ) , and to the broader use of LLMs as evaluators ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . The primacy we document is not unique to our stimuli: similar early-option preferences arise in a separately constructed, position-counterbalanced admissions benchmark ( Echterhoff et al., 2024 ) , and preference-manipulation attacks succeed more often when their wording overlaps with the user’s request ( Nestaas et al., 2024 ) . Two findings bear directly on reading a price equivalent off a prompt. Demand curves elicited from GPT-3 are broadly downward-sloping but generally not monotone in price ( Brand et al., 2023 ) . In blinded LLM simulations, varying price across otherwise comparable prompts can systematically alter the model’s implicit assumptions about unspecified pre-treatment characteristics and competing-product prices, which violates unconfoundedness ( Gui and Toubia, 2025 ) . We address both in Section 3 : position and cue target are counterbalanced within every cell (Section 3.2 ), and we read PE as a prompt-conditional threshold rather than a structural preference parameter (Section 3.1 ). 3. Method We frame PE auditing as a reusable auditing protocol with three components: a counterbalanced, position-controlled price sweep that yields the price-equivalent (Section 3.1 ); a cue-free price-sensitivity control that calibrates cross-model comparison (Section 4.4 , Appendix E ); and a primacy diagnostic that guards choice-based readings (Section 3.2 , Section 4.5 ). The protocol applies unchanged to any seller-controlled intervention, model, or category; we instantiate it here on marketing cues across two categories and seven models (Table 1 ). 3.1. Task, price-equivalent, and estimation A pair is two products matched on price, star rating, rating count, and specifications. One product carries a cue and the other does not. In a two-alternative forced choice, we first record P ⁡ ( choose cued ) P(\text{choose cued}) at equal price. We then raise the cued product’s price step by step, so that it costs a fixed percentage more than its otherwise identical counterpart. This premium runs across eight levels from 0 0 to 26 % 26\% ( 0 0 , 2 2 , 4 4 , 6 6 , 8 8 , 12 12 , 18 18 , and 26 % 26\% ) and is spaced more finely near zero, where most crossings fall. The 26 % 26\% ceiling is an empirical bracket, not a fixed constant. It sits above the largest price-equivalents we observe (the strongest cues cross near 13 13 – 22 % 22\% ), so the crossing falls inside the window for all but a few cues. We report those few as right-censored lower bounds ( † \dagger ). Premia beyond 26 % 26\% would add no crossing information, because by then even the strongest cue is almost always abandoned. The cue’s price-equivalent (PE) is the premium g ∗ g^{\ast} at which the cued product’s selection share falls to one half ( P = 0.5 P{=}0.5 ): how much more expensive the cued product may be before the agent abandons it, reported in percent of base price. Formal definition. Fix a model and prompt environment M M and a product-pair distribution Q Q . For each internally labelled pair ( x A , x B ) (x_{A},x_{B}) , let Z = ( T , R ) ∈ { A , B } × { 1 , 2 } Z=(T,R)\in\{A,B\}\times\{1,2\} specify which product receives the cue and price premium ( T T ) and whether that target is displayed first or second ( R R ). The presentation policy is the auditor-chosen probability mass function π \pi on these four states; it is not the model’s decision policy. Our balanced policy sets π ⁡ ( A , 1 ) = π ⁡ ( A , 2 ) = π ⁡ ( B , 1 ) = π ⁡ ( B , 2 ) = 1 4 \pi(A,1)=\pi(A,2)=\pi(B,1)=\pi(B,2)=\tfrac{1}{4} . For a contrast c 1 : c 0 c_{1}\!:\!c_{0} (the comparator receives c 0 c_{0} : no sentence, a matched neutral sentence, or the opposite framing), let S Q ( g ∣ c 1 : c 0 , M , π ) S_{Q}(g\mid c_{1}\!:\!c_{0},M,\pi) be the probability that the model selects the c 1 c_{1} -bearing target when it carries proportional price premium g g over the c 0 c_{0} -bearing comparator, averaging over product pairs, the four states using weights π \pi , and generation randomness. We define its price-equivalent as PE Q ( c 1 : c 0 ∣ M , π ) = inf { g : S Q ( g ∣ c 1 : c 0 , M , π ) ≤ 1 2 } . \mathrm{PE}_{Q}(c_{1}\!:\!c_{0}\mid M,\pi)=\inf\bigl\{\,g:S_{Q}(g\mid c_{1}\!:\!c_{0},M,\pi)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bigr\}. PE is therefore the smallest proportional premium at which the target’s policy-averaged selection share falls to parity; we report PE as a percentage. It is conditional on the cue contrast, audited products, presentation-policy weights, model, prompt, and decoding configuration; it should not generally be interpreted as individual indifference or willingness to pay (Appendix B ). Table 1. Experimental setup at a glance. Models 8 LLMs, 4 providers (strong/weak pairs); GPT-4o reference Working sets 7 (aggregate figures); 6 (cross-model claims) Categories headphones and coffee machines, 6 pairs each Price sweep 0 0 – 26 % 26\% , 8 premia ( 0 , 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 12 , 18 , 26 0,2,4,6,8,12,18,26 ) Repetitions N = 24 N{=}24 per (pair, price-point) Per condition 6 × 8 × 24 = 1152 6\times 8\times 24=1152 trials Total 113,472 113{,}472 trials Decoding temperature 0.7 0.7 Counterbalancing position and cue target, each 50 / 50 50/50 Robustness 4 task paraphrases (cue subset) Estimator model-free 0.5 0.5 -crossing; pair-clustered bootstrap CI Table 2. Core cue sentences (full set in Appendix A ). Cue Sentence appended to the cued product Social proof — weak “A popular choice.” Social proof — moderate “Chosen by over 1,000 customers.” Social proof — strong “Our best-selling model, chosen by over 10,000 customers.” Social proof — very strong “The #1 best-selling model, chosen by over 100,000 customers.” Scarcity “Only a few left in stock.” Authority “Recommended by audio experts.” Gain/loss framing “9 out of 10 buyers keep it.” (cued) vs. “1 out of 10 buyers returns it.” (control) Our primary estimator is model-free. It locates the point where the pooled P ⁡ ( choose cued ) P(\text{choose cued}) curve crosses 0.5 0.5 by linear interpolation between the two neighbouring price points (details in Appendix B ). Because position is counterbalanced within every (pair, price-point) cell (Section 3.2 ), this pooled curve is position-neutral in expectation. It therefore estimates choice behavior under a balanced ( 50 / 50 50/50 ) option-order policy, not a position-free preference. The estimator also needs no parametric form. This matters because cues routinely saturate the equal-price choice ( P = 1 P{=}1 ), which distorts a global logistic fit. The sweep is non-negative, so PE is identified only for cues that do not disadvantage the cued product. Two cases are therefore censored. If a cue is already dispreferred at equal price (equal-price choice rate, hereafter base rate , < 0.5 {<}0.5 ), we report PE ≤ 0 \leq 0 and flag it ( ‡ \ddagger ), and the base rate gives the identified sign. If the curve never reaches 0.5 0.5 within the sweep, PE is right-censored to a lower bound ( † \dagger ). For 95 % 95\% CIs we use a nonparametric bootstrap resampled by product pair ( Efron and Tibshirani, 1993 ) . With six pairs per condition, this small-cluster regime can make such intervals anti-conservative, that is, too narrow ( Cameron and Miller, 2015 ) . A position-controlled logistic fit and a price × \times position interaction check agree with the model-free values within about 3 3 points wherever a crossing is identified (Appendix D ). Interpretation. A stronger willingness-to-pay reading would require a specified user, a budget constraint, and a utility model with a truth-inducing payoff, as in discrete-choice WTP estimation ( Reusens et al., 2026b ) . Our measure requires only that the agent trades price against the cue when it forms its recommendation. We vary price within a single trial across two fully specified, visible product cards. The reference product’s price is displayed and held constant, so the swept gap is the only quantity that moves. This avoids the between-prompt channel by which price variation can silently shift unspecified covariates in blinded LLM simulations ( Gui and Toubia, 2025 ) . It does not rule out that a model reads price itself as a quality signal. We treat this as a matter of interpretation rather than a design confound. 3.2. Position control Agents over-select the first-presented option (Section 4.5 ), which near the parity crossing can bias PE. Within every (pair, price-point) cell we therefore counterbalance both position (the cued product is first in exactly half of trials) and cue target (the cue sits on product A and B equally often), with six calls in each of the four target–position states per cell, ruling out slot- and product-identity confounds. 3.3. Experimental setup: cues, stimuli, models, and protocol Cues. Cues are single sentences appended to a product’s neutral description. Price, rating, and specifications stay untouched, so a cue competes only through its wording. We draw on several persuasion families. Social proof comes in four intensities, which serve as a dose-response calibration. Scarcity and authority enter as single sentences. Framing pairs hold information constant and vary only its form (percentage vs. fraction, a rescaled rating, and a gain/loss framing), so any premium reflects form rather than content. Three kinds of controls complete the set. Neutral and vacuous sentences test content-free additions. In a length control, a cue competes against a neutral sentence of matched length, which separates content from the mere presence of an added sentence. In a presence control, that neutral sentence competes against a second neutral sentence and should command no premium. Table 2 shows the exact sentences of the core cues. To study composition, we also measure one pre-specified sub-ceiling cue per family (social proof, authority, scarcity), singly and combined (Section 4.3 ). Stimuli. Stimuli are matched product pairs in two categories: six headphone pairs ($59.99–$199.99) and six coffee-machine pairs ($49.99–$299.99). Each neutral description was checked for persuasive content by an LLM judge on nine persuasion dimensions (headphones) and by a manual read of all pairs (Appendix N ). Models. We audit eight LLMs from four providers, each as a strong/weak pair: GPT-4o / GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet / Haiku, Nova Pro / Micro, and Llama-3.3-70B / 3.1-8B. GPT-4o is the reference model on which the full condition set runs. Two exclusions define the working sets used throughout. Nova Pro is dropped for a high non-response rate, which leaves the seven models of the main dataset over which we report aggregate figures (e.g. the headline trial count). The position-driven Llama-3.1-8B is additionally excluded from cross-model claims , which leaves the six task-engaged models those claims rest on. We additionally audit Jev , a decision-native model that returns a choice probability rather than text, with the same protocol (Section 4.7 ). Protocol. Each trial presents two product cards. Each card lists name, price, star rating, rating count, and description, and the cue is appended to the cued card’s description. A neutral instruction asks for a single option label: “A customer wants to buy {category}. Based on the two options shown, which would you recommend? Reply with only ‘Left’ or ‘Right’.” We parse the label by first-mentioned word match and treat unparsable replies as non-responses. We sample at temperature 0.7 0.7 with N = 24 N{=}24 repetitions per (pair, price point). One condition is therefore 6 × 8 × 24 = 1152 6\times 8\times 24=1152 trials, and the full audit totals 113,472 113{,}472 trials. Because the estimate is read from a prompt, we re-measure a cue subset under four semantically equivalent task paraphrases (Appendix J ). Exact wordings and model identifiers are in Appendix A , and the neutrality rubric is in Appendix N . All prompts, seeds, analysis code, and per-trial logs are available at https://github.com/Flexxbo/price-equivalent-auditing (Appendix O ). 3.4. PE auditing in practice The protocol is meant to be re-run on new interventions, models, and categories, so we state the five operating rules our own results force. (1) Counterbalance position and cue target within every (pair, price-point) cell (Section 3.2 ). A first-option lean of the size we document (Section 4.5 ) otherwise leaks into the estimate, and the pooled value is the crossing of the averaged curves, not the mean of the per-order crossings. (2) Read the equal-price base rate as a two-sided validity gate. A rate near 0.5 0.5 on every cue signals a model that does not engage the task, and we exclude such a model from cross-model claims (Llama-3.1-8B, Section 4.4 ). For an engaged model, a rate near 0.5 0.5 on a single cue means that cue has no detectable pull (PE ≈ 0 \approx 0 ). A rate of exactly 1.00 1.00 signals an axis with no resolution left, where the cue’s pull is unidentified rather than high (authority on three models, Section 4.4 ). The gate fails at both ends. (3) Always run the cue-free price-only control alongside the sweep. PE combines cue pull with price sensitivity (under the single-index model of Appendix B it is exactly their ratio), so a raw magnitude is uninterpretable on its own, and a cross-model comparison of raw PE compares two things at once (Appendix E ). (4) Make censoring explicit. A cue dispreferred at equal price is floor-censored ( ‡ \ddagger ); a curve that never crosses within the sweep is right-censored ( † \dagger ). A censored cell is a bound, not a value, and must not enter a ranking as one (Section 3.1 ). (5) Read PE as ordinal-to-interval. Rankings and coarse magnitude bands survive task rephrasing and re-sampling; exact percentages drift by a few points across phrasings and vary widely across product pairs (Section 4.6 , Appendix F and Appendix J ). 4. Results Unless noted, results are on the reference model (GPT-4o), position-controlled, with the model-free estimator and pair-clustered bootstrap 95 % 95\% CIs. 4.1. A cue’s price, and why a choice rate under-resolves it At equal price the agent chose the strong social-proof product in 100 % 100\% of trials ( 144 / 144 144/144 ), and kept choosing it well into the positive-premium range. Its price-equivalent is ≈ 13 % \approx 13\% ( ≈ $ 17 \approx\$17 on a $130 item): the model-free estimator gives 12.9 % 12.9\% (CI [ 10.9 , 17.1 ] [10.9,17.1] ). An equal-price choice rate saturates, so a single-point audit cannot separate cues that a price axis resolves. A strong social-proof cue and a neutral factual sentence are each chosen in ≈ 100 % \approx 100\% of trials at equal price, so they are indistinguishable at the ceiling. The price sweep, however, separates them cleanly. The neutral sentence is abandoned almost immediately ( ≈ 2 % \approx 2\% premium), while social proof holds to ≈ 13 % \approx 13\% . A single equal-price rate loses this sixfold difference (Figure 2 ). The resolving power comes from the price intervention, not from PE per se: any audit that adds a common cardinal axis escapes the ceiling, whereas a single equal-price rate cannot. This divergence between choice and price echoes a long-documented human dissociation between choice and valuation, in which the two elicitations weight attributes differently and can even reverse ( Lichtenstein and Slovic, 1971 ; Tversky et al., 1988 ) . A price axis thus recovers a valuation signal that a choice-rate audit discards. The agents’ priced profile is nonetheless not a copy of the human one. Figure 2. Both cues win ≈ 100 % \approx 100\% at equal price; the sweep separates them (crossings at ≈ 2 % \approx 2\% and ≈ 13 % \approx 13\% ). Two curves of P(choose cued) versus price premium (0–26\%): both start near 1.0 at equal price; the neutral sentence crosses 0.5 near 2\% and strong social proof near 13\%. Across the battery the failure is not only one of resolution. Figure 3 plots every cue condition in two coordinates: the equal-price choice rate a conventional audit would report, and the price-equivalent. Six conditions sit at a base rate of 0.95 0.95 or above and are thus indistinguishable on the conventional axis. Priced, they span nearly 20 20 percentage points, from 1.6 % 1.6\% to 21.4 % 21.4\% . In the notation of Section 3.1 , these conditions share S Q ​ ( 0 ) ≥ 0.95 S_{Q}(0)\geq 0.95 , yet their price-equivalents PE Q \mathrm{PE}_{Q} differ by an order of magnitude: equal selection share at g = 0 g{=}0 , very different price. More sharply, the two axes disagree on order. Scarcity is chosen more often at equal price ( 0.95 0.95 ) than a gain/loss framing ( 0.72 0.72 ), yet its premium is fourteen times smaller ( 1.6 % 1.6\% vs. 22.3 % 22.3\% , disjoint intervals). A choice-rate audit therefore ranks the two the wrong way round. 2 2 2 The gain/loss condition is two-sided: both cards carry a matched form of the same fact, so its base rate reflects a choice between two framings rather than a cue against nothing. The ordering against scarcity is unaffected. This is not a precision problem that more trials would fix. The two quantities measure different things: how often a cue wins when price is tied, and how much price it can absorb. A cue can be broad and shallow (scarcity) or narrow and deep (gain/loss framing). Only the price a cue can absorb is what a seller can convert into money. 4.2. Construct validity and a selective susceptibility profile A social-proof series of increasing intensity yields a monotonically rising, sharply nonlinear price-equivalent ( 0.7 < 1.3 < 12.9 < 21.4 % 0.7<1.3<12.9<21.4\% ). Weak and moderate claims sit near zero, and the premium switches on only at the strong claim. This is evidence that the instrument tracks persuasive strength. The steps are separated in the price metric, not merely ordered by point estimates: the weak, moderate, and strong social-proof intervals do not overlap on headphones (Appendix C ). The levels co-vary wording, customer count, and superlatives, so the series is an intensity gradient as a seller would write it, not a single-factor dose.
